stem: A 38-year-old man with a 4-year history of bipolar I disorder is euthymic on lithium (level 0.7 mmol/L) and olanzapine 10mg daily. He presents with a 4-day history of acute psychotic mania — grandiose delusions, no sleep for 72 hours, disinhibited spending, and agitation. BMI 34, BP 138/88, QTc 450ms. Lithium level 0.5 mmol/L (he admits to missing doses). What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?
options: Increase lithium to achieve level 0.8-1.0 and continue olanzapine
Add haloperidol 5mg IM for rapid tranquillisation
Stop lithium and switch to valproate loading
Add aripiprazole 15mg to current regime
Increase olanzapine to 20mg daily and ensure lithium optimisation (increase dose, check adherence), with crisis/home treatment team support if possible
distractors_rationale: Increasing lithium alone is too slow for acute mania — it takes 7-14 days. An antipsychotic increase (or switch to a more effective one) is needed for rapid onset. Also, lithium should be optimised but not as the sole treatment.

Haloperidol IM is for rapid tranquillisation of an acutely agitated/aggressive patient — not necessarily indicated unless he is at immediate risk. This patient is manic but not described as aggressive and refusing oral medication. NICE CG185 recommends oral antipsychotics first.
There is no need to stop lithium (it should be optimised). Valproate loading is not indicated as first choice in this scenario.

Adding aripiprazole may help but increasing the current effective agent (olanzapine) to the maximum licensed dose (20mg) is more logical before adding a third drug. Aripiprazole could be an augmenting agent if olanzapine alone at 20mg fails.

CORRECT. For ACUTE MANIA in a patient already on lithium + olanzapine: (1) OPTIMISE EXISTING MEDICATION FIRST — increase olanzapine to 20mg daily (the max licensed dose) and optimise lithium (address adherence, increase dose to achieve level 0.6-1.0). (2) If inadequate response: consider adding a different antipsychotic (aripiprazole, haloperidol) or switching /augmenting. (3) NICE CG185: For acute mania, offer an antipsychotic FIRST-LINE. This patient is already on olanzapine 10mg — increasing to therapeutic antipsychotic levels is the most logical step before adding a new agent. Lithium optimisation (level 0.6-1.0) is also important for rapid response in mania. (4) Consider the clinical setting: if he has good support, the crisis/home treatment team can manage him at home. If there is high risk (aggression, disinhibited spending, self-neglect), hospital admission may be needed. (5) Olanzapine 10mg → 20mg: increased efficacy in acute mania, but monitor metabolic effects (BMI 34 — already high).
teaching_point: Breakthrough mania on maintenance treatment: (1) ASSESS ADHERENCE — this is the MOST COMMON cause (missed doses → subtherapeutic lithium level). (2) OPTIMISE the current mood stabiliser AND antipsychotic before adding new agents. (3) For acute mania: increase antipsychotic to maximum licensed dose. (4) LITHIUM: increase dose to achieve level 0.6-1.0. (5) If inadequate response after optimisation: add a different antipsychotic (aripiprazole, haloperidol) OR switch to a different combination. (6) ECT: effective for severe or treatment-resistant mania. (7) Physical health monitoring: metabolic effects, QTc, weight, hydration (mania + poor intake + hot weather = lithium toxicity risk). NICE CG185: 'For people who develop acute mania while on maintenance treatment, review and optimise their current medication before adding new drugs.'
source: NICE CG185: Bipolar disorder; Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines

stem:
Theme: Psychiatric Syndromes in Neurological Conditions

For each description, select the CORRECT SYNDROME:

A. Cotard's syndrome
B. Capgras syndrome
C. Fregoli syndrome
D. Intermetamorphosis syndrome
E. Subjective doubles syndrome
F. Reduplicative paramnesia
G. Ganser syndrome
H. Kluver-Bucy syndrome
I. Charles Bonnet syndrome
J. Anton syndrome
K. Frégoli syndrome
options: A 75-year-old woman with macular degeneration reports seeing detailed images of flowers and animals in her garden. She knows they are not real. She has no other psychiatric symptoms.
A 68-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease firmly believes his wife has been replaced by an identical-looking imposter. He is distressed and asks the police to investigate.
A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia believes that different people she meets are actually the same person, but in disguise — changing their appearance to follow her.
A 45-year-old man with bipolar disorder (manic episode) believes he has died and no longer exists, that his internal organs are rotting, and that he is a walking corpse.
distractors_rationale: CHARLES BONNET SYNDROME (I). Visual hallucinations in people with SIGNIFICANT VISUAL IMPAIRMENT (macular degeneration, glaucoma, cataracts, diabetic retinopathy). Key features: (1) COMPLEX, well-formed, often vivid visual hallucinations (people, animals, patterns, landscapes); (2) FULL INSIGHT — the person KNOWS the images are not real (distinguishes it from psychotic hallucinations); (3) NO other psychotic symptoms (no delusions, thought disorder); (4) No cognitive impairment (not dementia). Treatment: (1) Reassurance (the benign nature, the preservation of insight); (2) Optimise vision (cataract surgery, improve lighting, magnification aids); (3) Medication: low-dose antipsychotics (risperidone or haloperidol) ONLY if extremely distressing; (4) CBT can help with coping strategies. Prevalence: up to 10-15% of elderly with severe visual impairment. The hallucinations can range from simple (patterns, dots) to complex (scenes).

CAPGRAS SYNDROME (B). The delusional belief that a CLOSE PERSON (spouse, parent, child) has been replaced by an IDENTICAL- LOOKING IMPOSTER. It is a DELUSIONAL MISIDENTIFICATION SYNDROME. The person looks the same but is 'not the real one.' Can occur in: (1) NEURODEGENERATIVE DISEASES (Alzheimer's — most common cause in elderly, associated with right frontotemporal and right temporal damage); (2) SCHIZOPHRENIA (usually paranoid); (3) TBI, dementia with Lewy bodies, stroke. Pathophysiology: disruption of the connection between FACE PROCESSING (temporal lobe) and AFFECTIVE RESPONSE (amygdala/limbic) — the person recognisess the face but lacks the FEELING OF FAMILIARITY. The cognitive system then creates a DELUSIONAL EXPLANATION ('It's an imposter'). Management: (1) Treat the underlying condition; (2) Antipsychotics (if psychotic); (3) Re-orientation, validation therapy; (4) Avoid arguing with the delusion.

FREGOLI SYNDROME (C). The delusional belief that DIFFERENT PEOPLE are actually THE SAME PERSON in DISGUISE. The person believes that a persecutor (or other person) is following them, constantly changing their appearance to avoid detection. Named after the Italian actor Leopoldo Fregoli, who was famous for his quick-change artistry. Associated with: schizophrenia (paranoid), delusional disorder, dementia, TBI. Note: there is a typographical and mnemonic difference — FREGOLI (people are the same person in disguise) vs CAPGRAS (a person is replaced by an imposter). Both are DELUSIONAL MISIDENTIFICATION SYNDROME.

COTARD'S SYNDROME (A). The nihilistic delusion that one is dead, does not exist, or has lost their internal organs or identity. The 'walking corpse' syndrome. Associated with: (1) PSYCHOTIC DEPRESSION (most common — should be screened for); (2) SCHIZOPHRENIA; (3) DEMENTIA; (4) TBI; (5) Neurological conditions (parietal lobe). The patient may also believe they are immortal (although dead), cannot die, or have rotting organs. Management: (1) Treat underlying depression (ECT is VERY effective — 80-90% response); (2) Antidepressants + antipsychotics; (3) ECT should be considered early. Cotard's + Capgras can co-occur. Pathophysiology: parietal lobe involvement (metabolic mismatch between the 'self' and the world). Risk: extreme self-neglect, refeeding syndrome, suicide.
teaching_point: Delusional misidentifcation syndromes — HIGH-YIELD for MRCPsych: (1) CAPGRAS: person replaced by imposter (face processing WITHOUT emotional recognition). (2) FREGOLI: different people are same person in disguise (the 'persecutor' is everywhere). (3) COTARD'S: I am dead/ do not exist (nihilistic). (4) CHARLES BONNET: visual hallucinations due to blindness (with insight). (5) KLUVER-BUCY: bilateral temporal lobe damage — hyperorality, hypersexuality, disinhibition, visual agnosia, hypermetamorphosis, placidity. (6) ANTON SYNDROME: cortical blindness with denial of blindness (patients CONFABULATE what they see — bilateral occipital damage). (7) GANSER SYNDROME: 'approximate answers' (e.g., 2+2=5) — associated with prison populations/ malingering — also called 'prison psychosis' or pseudodementia. (8) REDUPLICATIVE PARAMNESIA: belief that a place has been duplicated (e.g., 'This hospital has a twin in another city'). Management of ALL misidentification delusions: (1) Treat the underlying condition; (2) ECT for Cotard's + depression; (3) Antipsychotics for schizophrenia; (4) Don't argue with the delusion — validate feelings.
source: Capgras J & Reboul-Lachaux J (1923); Cotard J (1880); Fleetwood R et al. (2014) Delusional misidentification; DSM-5-TR

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a 10-year history of treatment-resistant depression (failed 4 antidepressants + CBT + rTMS) is referred for consideration of ECT. She has severe depression with melancholic features, poor oral intake (weight loss 15kg over 6 months), and passive suicidal ideation. MMSE is 27/30 (normal). She has a history of myocardial infarction 8 months ago and atrial fibrillation (rate-controlled on bisoprolol). She is on apixaban. She has no prior experience with ECT. Which of the following is TRUE regarding ECT in this patient?
options: ECT is contraindicated due to the recent MI and apixaban — the cardiac risk is too high
ECT can be considered but apixaban must be stopped and bridged with heparin before treatment, and a cardiology assessment is required
ECT is the treatment of choice for severe depression with poor oral intake and treatment resistance — the risks are acceptable with appropriate anaesthetic and cardiac monitoring
ECT is only effective for psychotic depression, not melancholic depression
rTMS was more likely to work than ECT
distractors_rationale: Recent MI is NOT an absolute contraindication to ECT. The NICE TA136 guideline supports ECT use when the severity of depression outweighs the risks. With appropriate anaesthetic assessment and cardiology review, ECT can be performed safely after MI (usually waiting 3-6 months). This patient is 8 months post-MI.

Apixaban (DOAC — Direct Oral Anticoagulant) does NOT need to be bridged with heparin for ECT. ECT is a NON-INTERVENTIONAL procedure (no surgical incision). The standard approach is: (1) Check the indication for apixaban (AF — for stroke prevention); (2) The risk of THROMBOEMBOLISM if apixaban is stopped (stroke risk in AF) vs the risk of BLEEDING (intracranial haemorrhage with ECT — very rare, estimated <1/10,000). Apixaban should be CONTINUED for ECT because the bleeding risk is low and the stroke risk from stopping is significant. Some centres stop the morning dose or reduce to a therapeutic window — but bridging is NOT required.

CORRECT. ECT is the MOST EFFECTIVE treatment for severe depression, especially when: (1) TREATMENT-RESISTANT (failed 4+ trials); (2) POOR ORAL INTAKE / WEIGHT LOSS (need for rapid response due to nutritional compromise); (3) MELANCHOLIC features; (4) HIGH SUICIDE RISK. Response rate ~60-80% for severe depression (80-90% for psychotic depression). The patient is 8 months post-MI — acceptable for ECT with: (a) PRE-ECT CARDIOLOGY assessment; (b) ANAESTHETIC review; (c) ECG before each treatment; (d) Modified ECT with brief-pulse stimulation; (e) Apixaban CONTINUED (not stopped). The cognitive effects of ECT (mainly anterograde amnesia — transient) are a significant consideration, but the severity of her depression justifies the risk.
ECT is effective for BOTH psychotic and non-psychotic severe depression. It is NOT limited to psychotic depression. Response rates: psychotic depression 80-90%, severe melancholic depression 60-80%.
rTMS has not been tested against ECT for severe depression with poor oral intake. The evidence for rTMS is weaker than ECT for treatment-resistant depression.
teaching_point: ECT in the medically ill patient — deciding fitness: (1) CARDIOVASCULAR: recent MI (wait 3-6 months if possible), pacemaker (safe — consult cardiology), heart failure (optimise before ECT), QTc prolongation (monitor electrolytes). (2) ANTICOAGULANTS: DOACs (apixaban, rivaboxaban, edoxaban) CAN BE CONTINUED for ECT — no bridging needed. Warfarin: check INR ≤3.0 on day of ECT. Antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel): continue (low bleeding risk). (3) INTRACRANIAL: space-occupying lesion = CONTRAINDICATION (risk of brain herniation). (4) ECT is NOT contraindicated in: pacemaker, prosthetic valve, epilepsy (can be protective), pregnancy (safe with monitoring), Parkinson's (can improve motor function). Contraindications: increased intracranial pressure, recent intracerebral haemorrhage, unstable vascular aneurysm. Relative contraindications: severe osteoporosis, severe hypertension, phaeochromocytoma. Cognitive side effects: anterograde amnesia = resolves weeks-months; retrograde amnesia = may persist, especially for personal events around the time of ECT. Bitemporal ECT: more effective, more cognitive effects. Right unilateral ECT: fewer cognitive effects, less effective.
source: NICE TA136: ECT; BNF; Toot J et al. (2014) ECT in the medically ill; UK ECT Review Group (2003)

stem: A 14-year-old boy is referred with a 3-month history of difficulty concentrating at school, fidgeting, interrupting teachers, and forgetting homework. His parents confirm these behaviours have been present 'for years' across multiple settings. He has always been 'on the go.' What additional information is MOST important before making a diagnosis of ADHD?
options: An IQ test
A CONNERS parent and teacher rating scale AND a developmental history establishing onset of symptoms BEFORE AGE 12 with impairment across settings
An EEG
A trial of methylphenidate to see if symptoms improve
A family history of ADHD
distractors_rationale: IQ testing is not a diagnostic tool for ADHD — it helps identify learning difficulties but is not the key diagnostic step.

CORRECT. NICE NG87 (ADHD) diagnostic assessment requires: (1) A COMPREHENSIVE DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY — establishes onset before age 12 (DSM-5-TR) and identifies early signs; (2) RATING SCALES from BOTH PARENTS AND TEACHERS — the CONNERS rating scale is the most widely used (also SNAP-IV, Vanderbilt scale). Information from MULTIPLE SETTINGS is essential for DSM-5 'cross-situational' criterion; (3) SCHOOL REPORT — evidence of functional impairment; (4) COLLATERAL HISTORY — from parents, school, other professionals; (5) MEDICAL HISTORY — including birth history, head injuries, seizures, medications; (6) MENTAL STATE EXAMINATION; (7) RULE OUT alternative explanations (anxiety, ASD, trauma, sleep disorder, family dysfunction). The key: ADHD symptoms must be PRESENT IN MULTIPLE SETTINGS (home AND school) with clear evidence of ONSET BEFORE AGE 12. NICE NG87: 'Do not diagnose ADHD on the basis of rating scale scores alone — a comprehensive clinical assessment is required.'
EEG is not indicated for ADHD diagnosis unless there is a suspicion of seizures. There are no biomarkers for ADHD.

A trial of medication is NOT appropriate without first establishing the diagnosis. The NICE guideline emphasises: 'A full assessment should be completed before any medication is started.' Diagnosis must come first.
Family history is relevant (ADHD is highly heritable at 70-80%) but is not the most important diagnostic information — developmental history and cross-situational symptoms are key.
teaching_point: ADHD assessment in children — NICE NG87 approach: (1) REFERRAL: if symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity present for >3 months, causing impairment across settings. (2) ASSESSMENT: by a specialist (child psychiatrist, paediatrician, or specialist nurse) with training in ADHD. (3) DIAGNOSTIC TOOLS: CLINICAL INTERVIEW + DEVELOPMENTAL HISTORY + SCHOOL REPORT + PARENT AND TEACHER RATING SCALES. (4) RATING SCALES (for screening, not diagnosis): Conners (3rd Ed), SNAP-IV, Vanderbilt ADHD Diagnostic Parent/Teacher Scale, Brown Executive Function/Attention Scales, Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ — good for screening). (5) DIFFERENTIALS: anxiety, depression, ASD, ODD, tic disorders, sleep apnoea, trauma (early adversity can mimic ADHD), hyperthyroidism, lead poisoning. (6) COMORBIDITY: ODD (50%), anxiety (25%), depression (20%), ASD (15%), learning difficulties (35%), tic disorders (10%). (7) INVESTIGATIONS: NOT routine — no blood/imaging for ADHD. BUT check: if there are concerns about: growth (height/weight centiles), sleep (sleep study if OSA suspected), seizures (EEG), learning (educational psychology assessment). DSM-5-TR: for adolescents 17+ and adults, only FIVE symptoms (not six) in each domain. The key point: ADHD is a CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS based on comprehensive history from MULTIPLE SOURCES.
source: NICE NG87: ADHD; DSM-5-TR; Conners CK (2008) Conners Rating Scales

stem: A 17-year-old girl with no significant medical history presents with a 6-month history of binge eating and purging (self-induced vomiting) 2-3 times per week. She is distressed by these behaviours. Her periods are regular. Her BMI is 23. She has no other psychiatric symptoms. She has not had any previous treatment. Which is the MOST appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Start fluoxetine 60mg daily
Refer for enhanced cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-E) — this is the most evidence-based psychological treatment for bulimia nervosa, recommended by NICE as first-line
Admit to an eating disorders unit
Start Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) + fluoxetine 60mg immediately
Refer for family therapy
distractors_rationale: Fluoxetine 60mg is recommended by NICE as an ALTERNATIVE to CBT-E (if the patient declines or does not have access to psychological therapy) or as a SECOND-LINE after CBT-E. But NICE recommends CBT-E FIRST-LINE for bulimia nervosa (NICE NG69).

CORRECT. NICE NG69 recommends: For ADULTS with BULIMIA NERVOSA, offer CBT-E (enhanced CBT for eating disorders) — this is the FIRST-LINE treatment. CBT-E is specifically designed for eating disorders by Fairburn and colleagues. It focuses on: (1) Breaking the binge-purge cycle; (2) Identifying triggers for bingeing; (3) Reducing dietary restriction; (4) Addressing shape and weight concerns; (5) Relapse prevention. Format: 16-20 sessions over 4-5 months. EVIDENCE: Response rate ~40-60% for cessation of binge-purge episodes at 1 year. If CBT-E is unsuccessful or not available: (1) Fluoxetine 60mg (NICE) alone or combined with a less intensive self-help CBT; (2) IPT for eating disorders (second-line). The majority of patients can be treated AS AN OUTPATIENT. Admission is RARELY needed for bulimia (unless there is severe medical instability — electrolyte disturbance, hypokalaemia, cardiac arrhythmia, or severe purging with risk of oesophageal rupture).

Admission is rarely needed for bulimia — this patient has no medical instability (normal BMI, regular periods, no mention of electrolyte disturbance). Admission is reserved for: BMI <15, rapid weight loss, severe electrolyte disturbance, high suicide risk, severe purging with medical complications.

Combined CBT + fluoxetine is not superior to CBT alone (NICE meta-analysis). The addition of fluoxetine does not significantly improve outcomes over CBT alone. It is reserved for those who do not fully respond to CBT.

Family therapy (FBT — Family-based Treatment) is the first-line treatment for ADOLESCENT ANOREXIA NERVOSA (NICE), not for bulimia in a 17-year-old. For bulimia in adolescents, CBT-E adapted for younger patients is recommended.
teaching_point: Bulimia nervosa treatment (NICE NG69) — stepped care: STEP 1: ASSESSMENT — confirm diagnosis (binge eating + compensatory behaviours, ≥1/week, 3 months). Assess medical risk: K+, ECG, dental health, parotid gland enlargement, calluses (Russell's sign). STEP 2: OUTPATIENT — CBT-E as first-line (16-20 sessions). STEP 3: If CBT-E declined/no access: offer SELF-HELP CBT (guided or pure self-help) OR FLUOXETINE 60mg (the only medication with a license for bulimia). STEP 4: If inadequate response: consider combined treatment (CBT + fluoxetine) or alternative therapy (IPT, DBT — for emotion regulation). STEP 5: ADMISSION — only if severe medical compromise (very low K+ <2.5, ECG changes (QTc, U wave), hypothermia, hypotension, severe purging with risk of Mallory-Weiss tear/oesophageal rupture). Key medical complications: HYPOKALAEMIA (most serious — causes cardiac arrhythmias, renal impairment), hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis (due to vomiting/laxative use), salivary gland hypertrophy, dental erosion (perimylolysis — acid from vomiting), Russell's sign (calluses on knuckles from self-induced vomiting).
source: NICE NG69: Eating disorders; Fairburn CG (2008) CBT-E; BNF
